documents.title: New Patient Preventive Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
27 y/o woman establishing care. Moved here this summer, 1st grade/2nd grade split classroom at a local elementary school. No complaints today. Feels well.

PMH: none. PSH: none. Meds: none, no supplements. Allergies: NKDA.
OB/GYN: G0. Regular cycles. Not currently trying to conceive, may in the next couple of years. Last Pap 2016 normal per old records.
FHx: mother - autoimmune hypothyroidism. Maternal aunt - rheumatoid arthritis. Paternal cousin - type 1 diabetes. No known cardiac disease or cancer.
SH: married, never smoked, doesn't drink, no drugs. Walks most days, some yoga.
Immunizations: HPV complete, Tdap 2014. Will get flu shot when available.

ROS: negative x 12 systems.

Exam: vitals as recorded, BMI about 23. Well appearing. HEENT normal, TM clear, oropharynx clear. Neck supple, thyroid normal size without nodules. Lungs clear. Heart regular, no murmur. Abdomen soft, no masses. Breasts: symmetric, no masses, no nipple discharge, no axillary nodes. Pelvic: normal external genitalia, cervix without lesions, Pap collected, bimanual normal. Skin: no rashes, no unusual pigmentation. Neuro nonfocal. Mood bright.

A/P: Healthy adult, preventive visit.
- Pap today (due, 3 years since last)
- CBC, CMP, lipids, TSH (family history of autoimmune thyroid disease), one-time HIV and hep C screen
- Discussed folic acid if she starts trying to conceive
- Flu shot in October
- RTC 1 year

Assessment/plan
1. Preconception: start folic acid 0.4 mg daily now (OTC, or a prenatal vitamin with that amount). Reviewed avoiding alcohol (already abstains), food safety, keeping flu and COVID up to date. 3. Health maintenance: Pap up to date (2019). Flu in the fall. Booster when eligible.

I've sent a referral to the OB group at the hospital; they usually do a first visit around 8-10 weeks and their office will call you to schedule. No alcohol (I know, not an issue), avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen, acetaminophen is fine if you need something. Call if you have bleeding or severe pain before then.

documents.title: Obstetric Discharge Summary
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
Admit 10/05/2022, discharge 10/07/2022.

Delivery: normal spontaneous vaginal delivery 10/05/2022 of a healthy term infant after an uncomplicated labor. Second-degree perineal laceration repaired in the delivery room immediately after birth. Placenta delivered intact. Blood loss within normal range.

documents.author: obstetrics

OB/GYN clinic - 10/10/2022

Seen five days after vaginal birth of her first baby. Delivery was complicated by a second-degree laceration, repaired right after delivery. She reports soreness at the repair and that urinating has been difficult and uncomfortable. She is nursing and would like to avoid any medication that might pass to the baby. No fever, no chills, no pus-like drainage.

Allergies: NKDA. Meds: prenatal vitamin.

Exam: afebrile. Perineum swollen with mild redness; no fluctuance, no separation of the wound edges, sutures intact. Urine dip negative for leukocytes, nitrites and blood.

Assessment: expected postpartum perineal edema with discomfort at an intact second-degree repair; dysuria from local swelling, no sign of infection.
Plan: sitz baths two to three times daily, ice packs, peri bottle with voiding, stool softening diet. No medications per her preference. Return for fever, discharge or wound opening. Routine postpartum visit as scheduled.

conditions.label: Nipple fissure due to improper breastfeeding technique

documents.title: Obstetrics Clinic Visit
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
OB/GYN - 11/04/2022

Reason: painful nipples with breastfeeding.

Kayla is 30 and about a month out from an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. Since the first weeks she has had pain in both nipples, sharp and burning, worst during feeds, with abrasions on both sides and some blood-tinged discharge at times. Baby is exclusively at the breast; no bottles or formula. She is worried this could be an infection or something wrong in the breast. No fevers, chills or body aches.

The perineal laceration has healed and is no longer bothering her.
Allergies: NKDA. Meds: prenatal vitamin. Never smoker, no alcohol.

Exam: both nipples red with small fissures. No breast erythema, induration or engorgement; no masses. Infant observed at the visit: well nourished, alert, active. Shallow latch noted with the feed.

Assessment:
1. Bilateral nipple fissures from poor latch
2. Exclusive breastfeeding, infant thriving
3. Healed second-degree laceration

Plan: latch and positioning reviewed in clinic; referred to our lactation consultant for hands-on help this week. Expressed breast milk to nipples after feeds and air dry. No signs of mastitis. Call with fever, a red or hard area of the breast, or worsening pain.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, high MDM

documents.title: Primary Care Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: exhausted, dizzy, losing weight.

S: 10 weeks postpartum, exclusively breastfeeding. Says she expected to be tired with a newborn but this is different - over the past several weeks she's gotten progressively more wiped out, lightheaded when she stands, and has dropped about 5 kg by her home scale beyond what she lost after delivery. Her mother noticed she looks tan, and she's seen it too: darker skin in the creases of her palms, along her laceration scar, and patches on her gums. No vomiting, no syncope, no fevers. Nipple soreness better since lactation help. Sleeping in pieces but mood okay.

Meds: prenatal vitamin/folic acid. NKDA.
FHx: mother autoimmune hypothyroidism, aunt RA, cousin T1DM.

O: BP low for her today, weight down as charted. Tired-appearing but not toxic. Hyperpigmented palmar creases, darkened scar, brownish patches on the gums. Thyroid normal. Heart regular, lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender. Breasts not examined today.
PHQ-9 5, mostly fatigue items.

A/P: Fatigue, orthostatic symptoms, weight loss and new hyperpigmentation postpartum - very concerned for primary adrenal insufficiency, autoimmune given family history. Postpartum thyroiditis and anemia also on the list.
- Drew BMP, 8 AM cortisol, ACTH, CBC, TSH this morning before any steroid
- BMP back before she left the building: Na 130, K 5.5. Fits.
- Called endocrinology on-call colleague; urgent consult arranged, likely Friday
- Strict precautions: vomiting, can't keep fluids down, fainting, confusion, severe abdominal pain -> ED immediately and tell them possible adrenal insufficiency
- Salt liberally, fluids
- Will call her with cortisol and ACTH

documents.title: Results Call
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Called pt. AM cortisol 3, ACTH 200 (resulted this morning). Together with low Na/high K, this is primary adrenal insufficiency until proven otherwise. Endo will see her tomorrow 10:30, confirmed with their office; faxed my note and labs. CBC and TSH normal. She's about the same as yesterday, keeping fluids down, no vomiting. Reviewed ED precautions again. She is breastfeeding - told her treatment is compatible with nursing.

medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth every morning on waking
Take 1 tablet by mouth every afternoon (around 2-4 PM)
Inject 100 mg into the thigh muscle once for vomiting, collapse or adrenal crisis, then call 911

documents.title: Endocrinology Consultation
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Endocrinology - New patient consultation, 12/16/2022
Referring: primary care

Dear Colleague,

Thank you for the urgent referral of Ms. Cronin, a 30-year-old teacher about ten weeks after her first delivery, who is breastfeeding.

History: progressive fatigue and lightheadedness over several weeks, about 5 kg of weight loss, and darkening of her skin most noticeable in the skin creases, her perineal scar and her gums. No vomiting or syncope. No prior steroid exposure.

Family history: mother with autoimmune hypothyroidism, maternal aunt with rheumatoid arthritis, paternal cousin with type 1 diabetes.
Allergies: no known drug allergies. Medications: prenatal vitamin.

Exam: BP 100/60 seated with a further drop and lightheadedness on standing (orthostatic). Pigmentation accentuated in the palmar creases and the scar; gingival pigmentation. Thyroid normal.

Data (drawn by you 12/14, 08:00): sodium 130, potassium 5.5, cortisol 3 mcg/dL, ACTH 200 pg/mL.

Impression: primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease). The combination of a very low morning cortisol with a markedly elevated ACTH, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and pigmentation is diagnostic; a stimulation test would add nothing and delay treatment. Autoimmune adrenalitis is most likely given the family history; 21-hydroxylase antibodies sent today.

Plan:
1. Hydrocortisone 20 mg on waking and 10 mg in the early afternoon. Fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily. Both are compatible with breastfeeding at these doses.
2. Sick-day rules taught and given in writing: double the hydrocortisone doses for fever over 38 C or illness needing bed rest, triple for more severe illness, until 24-48 hours after recovery. Vomiting or unable to take tablets = use the injection and go to the ED.
3. Hydrocortisone sodium succinate 100 mg IM emergency kit prescribed; she and her mother were shown how to use it.
4. Medical alert ID recommended.
5. BMP and renin in about 3 months; I'll see her then. Annual screening for other autoimmune endocrine disease (TSH at minimum) through your office is reasonable.

With thanks for involving me in her care.

medications.sig: Take 1 capsule by mouth 4 times daily on an empty stomach for 10 days

documents.title: Weekend Call
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Pt called my cell this morning. Since Thursday achy all over with chills, and now the outer part of her right breast is sore and pink, especially during feeds. Hasn't checked a temperature. No vomiting, eating and drinking. Started hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone yesterday per endo.

Sounds like early lactational mastitis. Sent dicloxacillin 500 mg QID x 10 days to her pharmacy. Keep nursing/emptying the right side, cool compresses after feeds. Per endo sick-day rules: double hydrocortisone (40 mg AM / 20 mg PM) while feverish or achy. If vomiting -> injection and ED. Asked her to see OB on Monday for an exam since they know her from the nipple issues; she'll call them first thing. Call me back if worse over the weekend.

documents.title: Obstetrics Acute Visit
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
OB/GYN - 12/19/2022, same-day visit

30 y.o. P1, about 11 weeks postpartum, breastfeeding, newly diagnosed primary adrenal insufficiency (started hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone 12/16; currently doubling hydrocortisone per sick-day rules). Four days of fever, malaise and a painful red right breast. It began with aches and chills and then localized breast pain with feeding. Her primary care physician started dicloxacillin two days ago and she has not improved.

Allergies: NKDA. Meds: hydrocortisone, fludrocortisone, dicloxacillin, prenatal vitamin.

Vitals: T 38.7 C (101.7 F), HR 88, BP 120/78.
Exam: right breast, upper outer quadrant - 5 cm area of firm induration with warmth and erythema; no fluctuance. No nipple discharge or retraction. No palpable axillary nodes. Left breast normal.

Labs today: WBC 12.0, CRP 18. Blood cultures drawn; no growth to date.

Assessment: right lactational mastitis not responding after 48 hours of dicloxacillin.
Plan: with no response to antibiotics, an abscess has to be excluded - breast ultrasound ordered for tomorrow. Continue dicloxacillin for now and continue nursing or pumping from the right. Keep stress-dosing hydrocortisone. ED tonight for rising fever, rigors, vomiting, lightheadedness or rapidly spreading redness.

medications.reason: Stress dose, adrenal insufficiency with febrile infection

medications.sig: Take 1 capsule by mouth 4 times daily for 10 days

results.text: Staphylococcus aureus, methicillin-susceptible (oxacillin susceptible). Heavy growth.

reports.text: Limited right breast ultrasound, upper outer quadrant, targeted to the palpable area. There is a complex, predominantly hypoechoic fluid collection with internal debris and surrounding hyperemia, measuring 5.0 cm in greatest dimension, with overlying skin thickening and edema. Reactive-appearing right axillary lymph nodes with preserved fatty hila. No solid mass.
reports.conclusion: 5.0 cm right breast upper outer quadrant fluid collection consistent with abscess in a lactating patient.

procedures.procedure: Incision and drainage of abscess, simple

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PHYSICIAN NOTE - 12/20/2022 06:15

HPI: 30 y.o. woman, breastfeeding a 2-month-old, with primary adrenal insufficiency diagnosed last week on hydrocortisone/fludrocortisone, seen by OB yesterday for right breast mastitis. Right breast pain and swelling have been building since 12/15 despite dicloxacillin since 12/17; fever and chills since yesterday, and overnight the breast became much more swollen. She has been doubling her hydrocortisone. No vomiting, no syncope.

Allergies: NKDA.
Meds: hydrocortisone 20 mg AM/10 mg PM (currently doubled), fludrocortisone 0.1 mg, dicloxacillin 500 mg QID, prenatal vitamin.
SH: teacher, never smoker, no alcohol.

Vitals: T 38.7 C (101.7 F), HR 102, BP 120/78.
Exam: uncomfortable, nontoxic. Right breast red and swollen with a tender, fluctuant 5 cm mass in the upper outer quadrant; tender right axillary nodes. Left breast normal. Lungs clear, heart tachycardic and regular.

Labs: WBC 14.0, Hgb 13.2, CRP 24.
US (bedside, read by radiology): 5.0 cm right breast abscess, UOQ.

MDM: lactational breast abscess with failure of outpatient therapy, febrile, in a newly diagnosed Addison patient - stress dose given before the procedure.

Course:
- Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at 06:50.
- General surgery consulted. Incision and drainage at the bedside under local anesthetic by surgery at 09:15: purulent fluid evacuated, loculations broken up, cavity irrigated and packed. Culture sent.
- Tolerated well, pain controlled, tolerating PO.

Disposition: discharged home 13:40.
- Stop dicloxacillin. Start cephalexin 500 mg QID x 10 days.
- Continue sick-day doubling of hydrocortisone until 48 h afebrile, then usual dose.
- Keep nursing or pumping from both sides; milk from the right is safe for the baby.
- Packing care reviewed; general surgery clinic wound check 12/28.
- Follow up with PCP this week. Return for fever not improving in 48 h, vomiting, spreading redness, or lightheadedness.

documents.title: ER yesterday
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Ended up in the ER yesterday morning - it was an abscess and they drained it and packed it. Now on cephalexin instead. Fever was down last night. They said to see you this week. Also, am I supposed to keep doubling the hydrocortisone?

documents.title: RE: ER yesterday
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Got the ED record, glad they drained it. Yes, keep the doubled hydrocortisone until you've been fever-free for two full days, then go back to 20 and 10. Front desk will put you in tomorrow morning.

documents.title: Primary Care Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
F/u after ED 12/20 for R breast abscess s/p I&D, and new Addison's (endo 12/16).

Feels a lot better. Last fever Tuesday night. Taking cephalexin QID, no GI upset. Still on doubled HC since 12/17. Dizziness much improved since starting steroids. Nursing on both sides, pumping some on the R.

Exam: afebrile, BP better than last week. R breast: packing in place, incision clean, mild residual erythema UOQ receding from the marked borders, no new fluctuance. Skin still pigmented.

A/P
1. R lactational breast abscess, drained - improving. Finish cephalexin. Wound check with surgery 12/28. Culture pending from ED.
2. Primary adrenal insufficiency - responding. Afebrile >48 h tomorrow, so back to 20 mg AM / 10 mg PM tomorrow. BMP today to see where Na/K are on fludrocortisone.
3. Will call with BMP.

documents.title: Your results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Hi Kayla - a few results:
- Sodium and potassium are almost back to normal (136 and 4.7). The fludrocortisone is doing its job.
- The breast culture grew a common staph that is sensitive to cephalexin, so the antibiotic you're on is the right one.
- Endocrinology called: your adrenal antibody test is positive, which confirms the autoimmune type of Addison's we suspected. Nothing changes in your treatment.
Have a restful holiday, and see you in a couple weeks.

documents.body:
Kayla is back three weeks after the breast abscess drainage and a little over three weeks into treatment for Addison's.

She finished cephalexin 12/30. The incision closed over about a week and she has had no fever, redness or lumps since. Nursing on both sides without pain now; the cracked nipples healed after the lactation visits. Energy noticeably better, no lightheadedness on standing. Taking hydrocortisone 20 mg on waking and 10 mg at about 2 PM, fludrocortisone 0.1 mg in the morning. She carries the injection kit in the diaper bag. Hasn't ordered a medical ID yet.

PHQ-9 3.

A/P
1. Primary adrenal insufficiency, autoimmune (21-OH Ab positive) - improving on replacement. BMP today. Endo f/u in March. Reinforced sick-day rules: fever or vomiting means call us or endo same day.
2. Right lactational breast abscess with mastitis - resolved.
3. Nipple fissures - resolved.
4. Exclusive breastfeeding continues; infant doing well.
Refills: endo is prescribing for now; we can take over refills once she's stable.

documents.title: Endocrinology Follow-up
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Endocrinology follow-up, 03/13/2023

Dear Colleague,

I saw Kayla today, three months after starting replacement for autoimmune Addison disease (21-hydroxylase antibodies positive). She feels close to normal: good energy, no salt craving, no lightheadedness. The breast abscess you and the surgeons managed has healed. She used sick-day doubling appropriately during that illness and has not needed the injection.

Current: hydrocortisone 20 mg on waking, 10 mg early afternoon; fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily. NKDA.
Exam: BP normal without orthostatic change today; weight stable. Pigmentation fading.

documents.title: Endocrinology Follow-up and Intrapartum Plan
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Endocrinology - 08/27/2025, 33 weeks' gestation

Well, no symptoms of under-replacement. Same doses: hydrocortisone 20/10 mg, fludrocortisone 0.1 mg. NKDA. Electrolytes today normal. BP normal.

INTRAPARTUM STEROID PLAN (sent to OB and Labor & Delivery):
1. On admission in labor: continue usual oral doses while able to take them.
2. At onset of active labor (or before cesarean): hydrocortisone 100 mg IV, then 50 mg IV every 6 hours until delivery.
3. After delivery: resume oral hydrocortisone at double her usual doses (40 mg AM / 20 mg PM) for 24-48 hours, then back to 20 mg / 10 mg if well. Continue fludrocortisone throughout.
4. Vomiting, hypotension or unexpected fever: IV hydrocortisone and call endocrinology.

She has a copy. Postpartum visit with me 3-4 months after delivery.

33 y.o. G2P2 with autoimmune primary adrenal insufficiency, now one day out from an uncomplicated vaginal birth of a healthy term baby (10/17, 05:52). Her first pregnancy, three years ago, was when the breast abscess and the adrenal diagnosis happened. Intrapartum stress dosing given per the endocrinology plan; now on oral hydrocortisone at double dose with fludrocortisone.

S: some cramping, bleeding lighter than a period. Has had a few episodes of chills with shivering overnight. No chest pain, no shortness of breath, no headache. Nursing exclusively, baby latching well.

O: T 37.8 C (100 F), BP 120/75, HR 80, RR 16.
Fundus firm and nontender, just below the umbilicus. Lochia rubra, small, no clots. Breasts full, tender to palpation, no focal redness. Perineum intact. Calves soft. Remainder of exam unremarkable.

Outpatient Physical Therapy - Pelvic Health / Initial Evaluation, 01/20/2026
Referral: OB/GYN, dx diastasis recti abdominis

Subjective: 34 y.o., 3 months postpartum (2nd vaginal delivery), breastfeeding. Notices a midline bulge with sitting up and lifting her baby and car seat. No pain. No urinary leakage or pelvic heaviness. PMH: primary adrenal insufficiency on hydrocortisone/fludrocortisone. NKDA. Goals: lift kids and return to yoga without doming.

Objective: supine curl-up produces midline doming above the umbilicus; separation palpable along the linea alba above the umbilicus, softer tension at the umbilicus, no hernia. Pelvic floor screen normal. Lumbar ROM full.

Assessment: diastasis recti abdominis with impaired deep core recruitment and load transfer. Good rehab potential.

Plan: 1x/week for 8 weeks - breath and transversus abdominis activation, graded loading, lifting mechanics, home program. Avoid full sit-ups/crunches for now.
